THE YMCA OF GREATER MONTREAL AND THE YMCA OF GREATER MONTREAL FOUNDATION 


2003-2004 


The YMCA of Greater Montreal is a partnership of 
volunteers and staff committed to the fulfillment of 
people in spirit, mind and body and to the 
development of self-reliance in the individual and the 
community. 


Through its actions, programs and services, the 
YMCA of Greater Montreal reflects the needs and 
aspirations of the communities and works with 
individuals, local communities and communities in 
developing countries in achieving social justice and 
control of their environments.

THE YMCA OF GREATER MONTREAL AND THE YMCA OF GREATER MONTREAL FOUNDATION 


Using the major orientations of its Vision 2005 plan as a starting 
point, the YMCA of Greater Montreal has once again this year 
strengthened its presence at the heart of community life. The 
figures speak for themselves and the accomplishments are 
impressive. 


We invested strategically in our human resources, philanthropy 
and partnerships, as well as in our facilities and community 
action. We helped reinforce the national network of YMCAs by 
providing strategic and operational support to certain 
associations in eastern Canada. In addition, we devised the 
necessary means to ensure our long-term prosperity and growth 
by developing a new strategic plan for 2005-2008. This plan, which 
is based on the main objectives identified in Vision 2005, also 
contains concrete strategies and tactics. 


YMCA OF GREATER MONTREAL 


In fact, we have done everything possible to ensure that the 
YMCA can continue to play a leadership role in the community for 
a long time to come and remain a unifying crossroads that is open 
to all. Our goal is to provide support, so that everyone can find the 
helping hand they need to improve their quality of life. 


We measure the scope of our social and community role by the 
testimonials of people who go to the YMCA of Greater Montreal, 
be it members, participants, volunteers or donors. The following 
pages contain a few of these testimonials, which illustrate the 
place our community centres make for people who are seeking 
support and those who try to help. 


In closing, we wish to thank our staff for their warmth and 
know-how, which are so often mentioned by all. And, of course, a 
big thank you to our volunteers and donors, whose continuous 
generosity is so essential to our activities.

The role of the Foundation is to ensure long-term financial growing our 

support for the YMCA of Greater Montreal. Over the years, tte Endowment Fund 
Foundation has demonstrated the importance of its role, notably 

during the major revitalization campaign in 1999-2000, which through a targeted 


raised $20 million. fundraising 


This year, we committed ourselves to growing our Endowment Campaign, which 
Fund through a targeted fundraising campaign, which was was launched at 
launched at the Annual Heritage Club Dinner. The campaign got 

off to a great start with personal donations by Michael Novak, the Annual 

Chair of the Endowment and Planned Giving Committee, and H 

Foundation governor, John E. Cleghorn, and his wife Pattie. Since Heritage Club 
then, members of the Foundation’s Board of Directors have Dinner. 

demonstrated their leadership with generous pledges and gifts to 

the Fund. 


THE YMCA OF GREATER MONTREAL FOUNDATION INC. 
2003-2004 


The value of our Endowment Fund is now $3.6 million. We are 
confident that it will grow significantly as the campaign 
progresses and we continue to receive designated and 
undesignated gifts, both outright and in the form of charitable 
bequests and other planned gifts. We remain convinced that the 
YMCA of Greater Montreal must be able to rely on an Endowment 
Fund that will meet the needs of the community. 


There is no doubt that these efforts to assure the future of our 
organization will meet with a favourable response from our 
community leaders and the general public. For all the work 
accomplished again this year, we wish to thank our board 
members, the Foundation staff, our donors and all volunteers, 
especially those who work in our local and association-based 
campaign committees. 


Claude A. Garcia Marcel Coté 
Chair of the Board of Directors President 


GILLES BOURRET had a job. He was gainfully employed. Then, one day he ended up on the 
street after losing his job due to a “supply and demand” problem without his really knowing 
why. Someday, he hopes to understand what happened. In the meantime, after spending 
five years of his life killing time between nights in homeless shelters, 


he has rediscovered the 
comfort of a room of his 
own and three meals a day. 


Gilles admits that he would never have made it this far on his own. “It's not something | was 
looking for. It just happened.” He was helped by the two Dialogue community workers. It 
started with human contact, then came his room, social assistance, arranging and 
accompanying him to doctor's appointment, as well as ongoing support. For Gilles, the room 
is the base of it all. The future is limited to the short term for him. Gilles wants to start by 
having his vision problems fixed. After that, who knows? Reintegrating into society is not 
easy. He doesn’t know what the futu olds, but he is gradually regaining his self-confi- 
dence and moving forward. Thanks to the YMCA and, more specifically, to the patience of 
Réjean and Jacinthe, Gilles is, by his own admission, learning tolerance from them.

| Faced with failing grades and rejection by other students, SHEILA ROUSSEL-BAKHTIAR 
lived totally withdrawn from others. In an attempt to make her feel less isolated, Sheila’s 
mother signed her up for the Between School and Home program. Contrary to all 
expectations, Sheila chose to get involved. Today, the centre is like a second family to her. 
Everyone knows her... In meeting people who accept, motivate and help her, she has 
slowly regained confidence in herself. 


“My grades are 
better at school, 
| try harder and 
feel stronger. 


"7 | have successfully integrated into the school and made friends. I'm not afraid of people 
/ anymore.” Sheila is now a volunteer in the program for 9-12-year olds. The teenager who 
never spoke with anyone recently welcomed visitors at an open house. She also 
participated in the centre's youth exchange program, which took her to Newfoundland, and 
signed up for the young leaders program. Her dream is to go to Nicaragua as part of the 
YMCA’s international exchanges. Sheila’s mother sums it all up by saying, “I don't know 

» what would have happened if it weren't for the YMCA.”

BETWEEN SCHOOL AND HOME 


As a YMCA member for 25 years, BERNADETTE FREDETTE donates to the 
Hochelaga-Maisonneuve centre to enable other less fortunate people to benefit from 
everything the centre has to offer, just like she does. The YMCA enables her to stay healthy 
and meet people. She appreciates the warm welcome and family-like atmosphere at the 
centre. She also likes the intergenerational mix, and is pleased to see an increasing 
number of youth at her local centre. These are all things that Bernadette wants others to 
enjoy as well. “When | make a donation, | want my money put to good use. 


| am confident that the 
YMCA won't waste it.”

ALEX ADEMOKOYA is 13 years old. He started going to the Pointe-Saint-Charles centre at 
age 9 to do some exercise, because he was, by his own admission “too fat.” He 
immediately fell in love with basketball. Since then, he’s been training four times a week and 
ranks among the best players in Quebec. Alex likes the Y and all the activities it offers, such 
as weight training to stay in shape, as well as the Youth Centre and Help with Homework 
program. 


“When I'm having 
trouble with my 
schoolwork, that's 
where | go to 

get help.” 


He likes the people at the Y, who always encourage him to excel. He likes the atmosphere 
too, which is respectful and welcoming, regardless of age or income. And what if there 
were no YMCA? “I! would have stayed at home doing nothing, getting fatter and fatter.” 


CA OPENS ITS DO 


STEVE DICKSON started doing volunteer work with YMCA youth without really thinking too 
much about it. He wanted to help out one of his friends who is a basketball coach, and he 
just kept going every week. For Steve, team sports provide a great opportunity for youth to 
learn about life. “Sports are good for their development. They learn how to get along in a 
group, just like in society. 


They learn how to win 
and how to lose. And 
they learn about respect 
and making an effort.” 


In addition to coaching basketball, Steve teaches computer skills and graphics to youth. 
The YMCA plays a vital role in this community, where there are so many underprivileged 
families, by giving teens a recreational and meeting place other than the street. Moreover, 
according to Steve Dickson, the Pointe-Saint-Charles YMCA is unique. “It's a real 
community centre for the people in the neighbourhood with a spirit and atmosphere all its 
own.” Youth feel so comfortable here that many of them return when they're older to give 
back to the community by volunteering their time. 


NATHALIE DORIS arrived from France two years ago with her husband and 
eighteen-month-old daughter. She didn’t have a job and the toy-lending library served as 
the gateway for Nathalie and her daughter into the community. The toy-lending library, 
which is a veritable Ali Baba’s cave for her daughter, also enabled Nathalie to meet other 
parents and people in the community who helped her adapt to her new environment. For 
Nathalie, the program turned out to be much more than a mere toy-lending service. Children 
learn how to share and respect things. They are stimulated by the activities and learn how 
to socialize. Nathalie was so enthralled by this place where toddlers of all nationalities and 
social backgrounds mix seamlessly that she decided to trade in her member's status for that 
of a volunteer. What was once a hobby became a part-time job and a real passion for her. 
In fact, she has now decided to change careers and become a teacher. 


“The toy-lending library 
changed my life on both 
. the personal and 
“ professional levels. 


| have had a lot of encouragement and support, which has helped me gain the 
self-confidence | needed to go back to school.”

CAROLE TROTTIER has always been a volunteer. The children at the YMCA are what really 
made her want to invest her time and efforts there. Carole has continued volunteering,- 
because she is motivated by the centre's social and community values, as well as the 
sharing atmosphere there. “Being a volunteer at the Y is different. You don’t calculate it in 
hours, but in results. | feel at home here, surrounded by friends. Life is good at the Y.” Carole 
was also surprised at how the Saint-Laurent centre makes every effort to welcome 
volunteers who have the time and want to get involved. As a former chair of the Local 
Advisory Committee, she liaised between volunteers, members of the centre and 
management, in addition to working on the annual fundraising campaign and working with 
toddlers. When she sees them on the street, the centre's toddlers often run up to give her 
a hug. 


“| have found a community 
that works well, helps others 
and is good for me too.” 


She hopes that the YMCA will continue to be attuned to the needs of the local community. 


TINA AND CELINE are sisters. They are both autistic. Life isn't always easy for the Nguyen 
family. One of their parents had to stop working. The doors to daycares, camps and other 
services were closed to them... For their parents, the West Island YMCA was like the light 
at the end of the tunnel. During the summer months, the two girls attend the day camp, just 
like other children their age. The only difference between them and the others is that there 
is always a companion with the girls. The centre recruited and contributes to the 
companion's salary. In addition to having a break during the summer, the girls’ parents are 
thrilled to see Tina and Céline blossom through the stimulation of other children and the 
centre's many activities. The staff's warm welcome makes the Nguyens forget that they're 
in any way different from other families. “| can’t tell you how much | appreciate the YMCA. 


| wish that more autistic children 
could benefit from this kind of 
integration, and that more 
parents knew about It. 


| really hope that more funds are allocated to the care of children like ours,” says the girls’ 
father. 


DAY CAMP 


JOHN BULMER discovered the YMCA at age 9. He's 64 now. “| grew up with the YMCA 
philosophy. It taught me how to share—a skill | needed to succeed in life.” He goes to the 
West Island centre to stay in shape, and would never switch to another sports centre. He 
has visited YMCAs pretty much everywhere in the world and has always found the same 
friendly attitude. 


“There's a kind of happiness you 
just don't find anywhere else. It's 
just one big, happy family.” 


In fact, it's a family with toddlers and seniors, teens, disabled people, as well as some 
well-heeled and poorer members. John believes that you can’t always take in life. You also 
have to give back. He thinks it's normal to give, so the centre can be open to all, and for a 
team or program to have the necessary resources to work—the same way he thinks it's 
normal to help boost the morale of a youth who seems to be having problems.

ROSALIE VENDETTE dreamed of changing the world, without really knowing how or where 
to start. Three years ago, a friend of hers suggested that she take a YMCA training program 
on globalization and take action. 


“| feel like my life really 
only started three years 
ago. Ihe course was a 

real awakening for me.” 


Rosalie then formed a group of volunteers associated with international programs. The 
group’s goal is to strengthen north-south ties. Rosalie changed the way she lives by 
consuming less, using public transportation, buying fair trade products, making ethical 
investments, etc.... She has even reoriented her career to be more in line with her values. 
Rosalie focused on corporate social responsibility and has spent the past year working on 
promoting responsible investment through shareholders’ right to vote. “Everyone can take 
action, whatever the means. | cannot encourage it enough.” 


INTERNATIONAL PROGRAMS

NOT IGNORE AND INSPIRING SOLUTIONS AS 


EDUCATION 


ANDREE TOURIGNY speaks on behalf of herself and her husband, the late Paul Tourigny. 
He had made a bequest to the YMCA‘s international programs to establish an endowment 
fund called the Haiti Youth Fund. As the parents of seven children, the couple was 
convinced that 


“children are the 
country’s future.” 


Education always came first for Paul. He was appalled by the Haitian students’ lack of 
resources, which is why he directed his donation to Haiti, thereby enabling some students 
to get an education on site and help improve the quality of life of their fellow citizens 
through knowledge-sharing. In fact, Andrée believes that a society must be founded on 
sharing. “After all, the city is nothing but an extension of our house, our property and our 
street.” Paul found that same dedication to sharing at the YMCA while doing research on 
the origins and development of the YMCA. He liked the Y, because it was open to all—in a 
class-free and clan-free environment—and adapted its initiatives to the needs of the 
people who live around each centre. 


16 / 


SAMUEL LAZARUS died of malaria in January while working as a volunteer in a daycare in 
Ghana. After being a longtime camper at Kamp Kanawana, Sam became a staff member. In 
his capacity as counsellor, Sam was much appreciated for his kindness and dedication, as 
well as for his extraordinary ability to inspire and motivate children. Sam's co-workers and 
friends decided to pay tribute to this tireless ambassador of Kanawana by creating an 
award in his name. The award will be presented every year to a staff member who best 
exemplifies the Kamp Kanawana motto: 


Non Nobis Solum 


(Not for Ourselves Alone). 


KAMP KANAWANA 
fe GE 


To ensure that Sam's name remains associated with the camp he loved so much, his 
family has created THE YMCA KAMP KANAWANA SAM LAZARUS FUND. Both family and 
friends have contributed to the fund individually and through various events, such as a 
benefit hockey tournament that raised more than $9,000, Allison Leduc’s first marathon, as 
well as weddings and retirement parties. Every year, revenues from the endowment fund, 
which is now worth $22,000, will enable children from underprivileged families to attend the 
summer camp. Two children benefitted from the fund this past summer. Sam's family hopes 
that it will remind us all that out of tragedy can come hope and inspiration.

SOCIAL AUDIT OF THE YMCA OF GREATER MONTREAL 


IN 2003-2004, THE YMCA OF GREATER MONTREAL FACILITATED ACCESS TO ITS PROGRAMS AND FACILITIES FOR MORE THAN 
5,792 PEOPLE WHO WERE IN FINANCIAL DIFFICULTY. 


THROUGH ITS PROGRAMS AND ACTIVITIES, THE YMCA OF GREATER MONTREAL ALSO REACHED 134,088 PEOPLE IN 
2003-2004.

THE YMCA OF GREATER MONTREAL AND THE YMCA OF GREATER MONTREAL FOUNDATION 


INNOVATION, RESEARCH AND 
DEVELOPMENT FUND 


FOLLOWING THE DEVELOPMENT OF THE V/S/ON 2005 STRATEGIC PLAN, THE YMCA OF GREATER 
MONTREAL CREATED A FUND TO BRING YMCA SERVICES AND PROGRAMS TO MORE PEOPLE. 
THIS YEAR, A SUM OF $150,000 WAS ALLOCATED TO SUPPORT NEW INITIATIVES, AS WELL AS 
TO MAINTAIN THE RELEVANCE, EFFECTIVENESS AND QUALITY OF THE YMCA'S WORK IN THE 
COMMUNITY. THE PROJECTS SELECTED MUST PROMOTE YMCA MISSION AND VALUES AND 
MEET COMMUNITY NEEDS. THE PROJECTS WILL ALSO BE EVALUATED AT THE END OF THE 


YEAR.

ANNUAL GOLF TOURNAMENT 


THE 19™ ANNUAL GOLF TOURNAMENT, WHICH DREW 132 PEOPLE TO THE PINEGROVE 
GOLF CLUB IN SAINT-LUC ON MONDAY, MAY 31, 2004, HELPED RAISE $50,700. THE 
FUNDS WERE USED TO FINANCE SEVERAL YMCA YOUTH PROGRAMS AND ALSO 
CONTRIBUTED TO THE CREATION OF THE YOUTH LEADERSHIP PROGRAM.

THE YMCA OF GREATER MONTREAL AND THE YMCA OF GREATER MONTREAL FOUNDATION 2003-2004 


ENDOWMENT FUND 


LAUNCH OF A NEW CAMPAIGN AT THE ANNUAL HERITAGE CLUB DINNER 


This year’s annual event was marked by the launch of a fundraising campaign aimed at 
growing the YMCA of Greater Montreal Foundation’s Endowment Fund. Michael Novak, Chair of 
the Endowment and Planned Giving Committee, and John E. Cleghorn, a Foundation governor, 
along with his wife Pattie, both set the tone by making a personal donation of $50,000 each. They 
also encouraged those present to participate in the group effort by making an outright 
contribution or by planning a future gift in their will or through a life insurance policy. 


MARCEL COTE, RECIPIENT OF THE GABRIELLE AND MAURICE A. MASSE AWARD 


The award is presented every year to a person or couple who have made an outstanding 
contribution to the YMCA of Greater Montreal. This year, the award was presented to Marcel 
Coté, a YMCA volunteer for more than 25 years. Over the years, Marcel has dedicated © 
tremendous time and energy to the Downtown YMCA’s Local Advisory Committee, as well as to — 
the boards of directors of the YMCA and the YMCA of Greater Montreal Foundation, the latter of ~ 
which he will be the president until the end of this fiscal year. Marcel was also one of the 
masterminds behind the association's revitalization over the past decade. On behalf of everyone 
at the YMCA, we would like to take this opportunity to congratulate Marcel and thank him for his 
exceptional dedication. 


22 / 


ALLOCATION OF ENDOWMENT FUND REVENUES 


The YMCA of Greater Montreal Foundation Endowment Fund was established to ensure long- 
term support for the mission of the YMCA of Greater Montreal. Annual revenues will provide 
stable, long-term funding for the YMCA’s community programs. In 2003-2004, a sum of $42,200 
was used to fund specific programs in accordance with donor designations, for example, Kamp 
Kanawana and International Programs. The remaining revenues of the Endowment Fund enabled 
the Foundation to allocate $63,400 to special projects. This year, the project selection committee 
accepted eight applications for the funding of special projects. 


Alternative suspension (Multiple centres) $15,000 


Peer Help with Homework — After-school study program 


(Pointe-Saint-Charles) $15,000 
Café 3D (Du Parc) $12,000 
Covered Garden (Downtown) $10,000 
Y5550 video — Drug abuse prevention (Du Parc) $2,300 
Financial Fitness and Youth Matters (Notre-Dame-de-Grace) $7,000 


Documentation centre (International programs) $2,100
